changes.before: This chapter introduces the novel interpretability methods enabled by the split-stream representations. The guiding objects throughout are the stream functions $g$ and $h$ with $f = g - h$ constructed in Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu}: every method below reads the two streams \emph{separately} instead of only their difference. Section~\ref{sec:split_attribution_concept} develops the \emph{split-based} route --- attributing the decisions of a pretrained network through its \ac{dc} decomposition, yielding SplitCAM, SplitLRP and SplitGrad \parencite{hiddenMono}, together with the complementary by-design route of difference-of-convex input neural networks (DCINNs), in which the difference of two constrained networks is \emph{trained} directly and exhibits class-dependent stream sensitivities in the displayed MNIST examples. Section~\ref{sec:game_based_attribution} turns to the \emph{game-based} route of Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory}: rather than re-deriving the stopping and routing games, it collects the practical \emph{modes} --- the tunable knobs that turn the game equilibria into concrete attribution maps --- and the \emph{technicalities} of equivariant averaging that raise attribution quality.
changes.after: This chapter develops interpretability methods from the streams $g,h$ with $f=g-h$ constructed in Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu}. Section~\ref{sec:split_attribution_concept} reads the streams separately to explain pretrained networks through SplitCAM, SplitLRP and SplitGrad~\parencite{hiddenMono}. It also studies directly trained difference-of-convex input neural networks (DCINNs), whose MNIST examples exhibit class-dependent stream sensitivities. Section~\ref{sec:game_based_attribution} collects practical \emph{modes} that turn the game equilibria of Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} into tunable attribution maps, and the \emph{technicalities} of equivariant averaging that improve attribution quality.
changes.reason: Condense chapter roadmap; retain both post-hoc and directly trained routes, qualitative MNIST scope, and game modes/averaging.

changes.before: This section develops the split-based methods on a shared conceptual basis, then instantiates SplitCAM, SplitLRP and SplitGrad on a pretrained network and closes with the by-design DCINNs. Post-hoc attribution methods assign to every input feature a score quantifying its influence on a fixed network output. The established families include gradient saliency~\parencite{Simonyan2014}, deconvolution and guided backpropagation~\parencite{ZeilerFergus2014,Springenberg2015}, \ac{lrp} and deep Taylor decomposition~\parencite{Bach2015,Montavon2017DeepTaylor}, class-activation mapping~\parencite{Zhou2016,Selvaraju2017}, baseline-based methods such as Integrated Gradients and DeepLIFT~\parencite{Sundararajan2017,Shrikumar2017}, noise-averaged gradients~\parencite{Smilkov2017}, and perturbation- or surrogate-based explanations~\parencite{Ribeiro2016,FongVedaldi2017,LundbergLee2017,Kolek2023_ShearletX,Fel2023_EVA}. These methods explain predictions of the original network. This section identifies information loss in methods that propagate ordinary local derivatives at the evaluated input, and shows how the split-pair representation of Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu} preserves separate stream signals.
changes.after: Post-hoc attribution assigns each input feature a score for its influence on a fixed network output. Established families include gradient saliency~\parencite{Simonyan2014}, deconvolution and guided backpropagation~\parencite{ZeilerFergus2014,Springenberg2015}, \ac{lrp} and deep Taylor decomposition~\parencite{Bach2015,Montavon2017DeepTaylor}, class-activation mapping~\parencite{Zhou2016,Selvaraju2017}, baseline-based methods such as Integrated Gradients and DeepLIFT~\parencite{Sundararajan2017,Shrikumar2017}, noise-averaged gradients~\parencite{Smilkov2017}, and perturbation- or surrogate-based explanations~\parencite{Ribeiro2016,FongVedaldi2017,LundbergLee2017,Kolek2023_ShearletX,Fel2023_EVA}. These explain the original network. We identify signal loss in rules using ordinary local derivatives, then develop SplitCAM, SplitLRP and SplitGrad from the separate signals preserved by the split-pair of Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu}, closing with by-design DCINNs.
changes.reason: Merge duplicated roadmap into mechanism statement; preserve all cited method families and derivative-rule scope.

changes.before: A \ac{relu} gate transmits its pre-activation if it is positive and emits an exact zero otherwise. In the forward pass the \emph{magnitude} of a negative pre-activation is annihilated; in the backward pass the local derivative of the gate is zero, so no gradient traverses the neuron either. We call this the \emph{subthreshold signal loss}: the suppressed pre-activation is invisible to the output through this gate and to backward rules that retain its ordinary local derivative. For ordinary input gradients this can cause exact regional blindness.
changes.after: A \ac{relu} gate transmits positive pre-activations and otherwise returns zero, erasing their negative magnitude and blocking the local gradient. This \emph{subthreshold signal loss} hides the suppressed pre-activation from the output through that gate and from backward rules retaining its ordinary derivative. Ordinary input gradients can therefore exhibit exact regional blindness.
changes.reason: Merge forward/backward explanation while preserving its restriction to ordinary derivatives.

changes.before: Together, Proposition~\ref{prop:sensitivity_mass} and Corollary~\ref{cor:backward_invariant} express a conservation law: the difference of the stream sensitivities reproduces the original gradient exactly, while their sum is pinned to the input-independent quantity $W_{\mathrm{abs}}^{[l]}$. Where Proposition~\ref{prop:gradient_blindness} shows the original gradient collapsing to zero, the two combined stream gradients coincide: writing $\delta^{(l, s)} \coloneqq \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\delta^{(l, +, s)} - \delta^{(l, -, s)}\bigr)$ for the combined gradient of stream $s$, Corollary~\ref{cor:backward_invariant} gives $\delta^{(l, g)} - \delta^{(l, h)} = \delta^{(l)}$, so the vanishing of $\delta^{(l)}$ is precisely the equality $\delta^{(l, g)} = \delta^{(l, h)}$ of the two combined stream gradients --- their difference, the network gradient, is zero. The common value may itself be zero. The individual sensitivities $\delta^{(l, \pm, s)}$ need not equal $\tfrac{1}{2} W_{\mathrm{abs}}^{[l]}$; their deviation from that pattern-independent half-bulk records precisely the routing decisions taken at the \ac{relu} gates, including the inactive ones. For a feature connected to the output by a path of nonzero weights, the sensitivity-mass identity guarantees that at least one of the two non-negative partial sensitivities of each head is positive. It does not guarantee that a difference of partials, a combined gradient, or an attribution map is nonzero. For example, with $f(x)=\relu(\relu(x)+\relu(-x)-10)$ and the balanced input split, both heads are locally equal to $10$ near $x=1$ and both combined gradients vanish.
changes.after: Proposition~\ref{prop:sensitivity_mass} fixes the sum of partial sensitivities at input-independent $W_{\mathrm{abs}}^{[l]}$; Corollary~\ref{cor:backward_invariant} recovers the original gradient from stream differences. Define $\delta^{(l,s)}\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\delta^{(l,+,s)}-\delta^{(l,-,s)}\bigr)$. Then $\delta^{(l,g)}-\delta^{(l,h)}=\delta^{(l)}$, so regional blindness (Proposition~\ref{prop:gradient_blindness}) means equal combined stream gradients, possibly both zero. Individual partial sensitivities $\delta^{(l,\pm,s)}$ can differ from $\tfrac{1}{2}W_{\mathrm{abs}}^{[l]}$; these deviations record routing at active and inactive \ac{relu} gates. A path of nonzero weights from the feature to the output guarantees at least one positive partial sensitivity per head, but does not guarantee nonzero partial differences, combined gradients, or attribution. For example, with $f(x)=\relu(\relu(x)+\relu(-x)-10)$ and balanced input split, both heads equal $10$ locally near $x=1$, and both combined gradients vanish.
changes.reason: Merge conservation explanation and repeated zero-gradient restatement; retain counterexample and exact limits of positivity guarantee.

changes.before: \emph{SplitLRP} runs \ac{lrp} on the decomposed model, treating the positive and negative streams of each layer as two groups of neurons within one unified network. Accordingly, each layer carries \emph{two} relevance tensors $R^{(l, +)}$ and $R^{(l, -)}$, propagated jointly through the four weight blocks built from $\Wsig{l}{+}$ and $\Wsig{l}{-}$ that couple the streams. The propagation is initialized at the class-specific positive output $\act{L}{+}$ of the $g$-stream. Since \emph{all} weights of the decomposed model are non-negative, the $\gamma$-rule loses its purpose --- there are no negative contributions to de-emphasize --- and we use \eqref{eq:lrp_gamma_rule} with $\gamma = 0$ and $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$, i.e.\ the $\varepsilon$-rule, on the split-pair. SplitLRP treats the paired Maxout gates \eqref{eq:split_maxout_gate} as transparent in the relevance pass.
changes.after: \emph{SplitLRP} treats both streams as neuron groups in one decomposed network. Each layer carries relevance tensors $R^{(l,+)},R^{(l,-)}$, jointly propagated through the four coupling blocks built from $\Wsig{l}{+},\Wsig{l}{-}$. Propagation starts at the class-specific positive $g$-output $\act{L}{+}$. All weights are non-negative, so we use \eqref{eq:lrp_gamma_rule} with $\gamma=0$, $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$: the $\varepsilon$-rule needs no preference for positive over negative contributions. Paired Maxout gates \eqref{eq:split_maxout_gate} are transparent in the relevance pass.

changes.before: On the original network the $\varepsilon$-rule mixes signed contributions, and the resulting backward transport is a \emph{signed} measure on paths --- the source of the interpretability caveats discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:trajectory}. On the split-pair all contributions $\tilde{z}^{(l+1)}_{ij}$ are products of non-negative activations and non-negative weights, so up to the stabilizer the \ac{lrp} propagation matrices are genuinely stochastic: SplitLRP is a Markov chain on the doubled computational graph, and the pair $\bigl(R^{(l,+)}, R^{(l,-)}\bigr)$ is an honest, unsigned relevance measure. This is the same mechanism --- doubling the state space to absorb the weight signs --- by which the stopping game of Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} turns backward relevance flow into probability.
changes.after: The original network's $\varepsilon$-rule mixes signed contributions, producing a signed path measure (Chapter~\ref{ch:trajectory}). In the split-pair, $\tilde{z}^{(l+1)}_{ij}$ multiplies non-negative activations and weights. Up to the stabilizer, its propagation matrices are stochastic: SplitLRP is a Markov chain on the doubled graph, with unsigned relevance measure $\bigl(R^{(l,+)},R^{(l,-)}\bigr)$. Doubling the state space absorbs weight signs, as in the stopping game's probabilistic backward flow (Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory}).
changes.reason: Remove repeated emphasis around signed-versus-unsigned transport; preserve stabilizer qualification and game connection.

changes.before: The third method dispenses with activation weighting and relevance budgets altogether and uses the stabilized stream gradients themselves as the attribution signal. The stream functions consume a \emph{pair} of inputs, so we fix the balanced embedding $\act{0}{\pm} = \pm x/2$ and write $\tilde{g}^{(l)}(a) \coloneqq g^{(l)}\bigl( \tfrac{a}{2}, -\tfrac{a}{2} \bigr)$, $\tilde{h}^{(l)}$ analogously. By the chain rule (Section~\ref{subsec:backward_stabilization}) the unified stream gradient $\partial \tilde{s}^{(l)} / \partial a$ equals the combined sensitivity $\bigl(\delta^{(l, +, s)} - \delta^{(l, -, s)}\bigr)/2$, which justifies the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in \eqref{eq:shift_definition}: the combined shifted sensitivities $\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}^{(l, g)}, \delta_{\mathrm{shift}}^{(l, h)}$ are stabilized gradients of the convex functions $\tilde{g}^{(l)}, \tilde{h}^{(l)}$, and their difference always reproduces the exact original gradient, since the common shift in \eqref{eq:shift_definition} cancels sign-wise.
changes.after: SplitGrad uses stabilized stream gradients directly. For the paired-input streams, fix the balanced embedding $\act{0}{\pm}=\pm x/2$ and write $\tilde{g}^{(l)}(a)\coloneqq g^{(l)}\bigl(\tfrac{a}{2},-\tfrac{a}{2}\bigr)$, and $\tilde{h}^{(l)}$ analogously. The chain rule (Section~\ref{subsec:backward_stabilization}) gives $\partial\tilde{s}^{(l)}/\partial a=\bigl(\delta^{(l,+,s)}-\delta^{(l,-,s)}\bigr)/2$, explaining the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in \eqref{eq:shift_definition}. The combined shifted sensitivities $\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}^{(l,g)},\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}^{(l,h)}$ are stabilized gradients of convex $\tilde{g}^{(l)},\tilde{h}^{(l)}$; their difference recovers the exact original gradient because the common shift cancels sign-wise.
changes.reason: Condense balanced embedding/chain-rule explanation; preserve factor and exact difference invariant.

changes.before: The methods of Sections~\ref{sec:split_cam}--\ref{sec:split_grad} explain a \emph{pretrained} network by imposing the split structure post hoc. This raises a converse question: if the difference-of-two-streams representation makes explanations legible, what happens when the difference structure is not derived but \emph{trained} --- when the hypothesis class itself is the set of differences of two constrained networks? This section studies \ac{dc} input neural networks (DCINNs) and their monotone relatives. The displayed MNIST examples show class-dependent stream sensitivities on present strokes and candidate missing strokes, at a modest and architecture-dependent cost in accuracy.
changes.after: To study mechanisms exposed by the \ac{dc} decomposition of pretrained networks (Sections~\ref{sec:split_cam}--\ref{sec:split_grad}), we directly train small DC input neural networks (DCINNs) and their monotone relatives on MNIST. Their shared opposing-stream structure provides a controlled setting for examining class-dependent sensitivities on present and candidate missing strokes, with a modest, architecture-dependent accuracy cost.
changes.reason: Explicit latest user-requested framing, refined by root: directly trained small DCINNs study opposing-stream mechanisms exposed by post-hoc decomposition. The first sentence distinguishes directly trained MNIST models; downstream empirical/counterfactual caveats stay intact. Source-paper DICs.tex and counterfactual_features.tex consulted.

changes.before: Recall from Section~\ref{sec:convex_monotone_foundations} that an \ac{icnn}~\parencite{Amos2017} is a network with convex, monotone activation functions and non-negative weights in all layers except possibly the first, and that such a network represents a convex function; a network with monotone activations and \emph{all} weights non-negative represents a monotone function. Throughout this section we view \acp{icnn} as monotone networks acting on an affine transformation of the input, embodied by the unconstrained first layer.
changes.after: An \ac{icnn}~\parencite{Amos2017} has convex, monotone activations and non-negative weights except possibly in its first layer, and represents a convex function (Section~\ref{sec:convex_monotone_foundations}). Monotone activations with all weights non-negative give a monotone function. We view \acp{icnn} as monotone networks composed with the affine transformation of an unconstrained first layer.
changes.reason: Shorten recalled convexity and monotonicity conditions; preserve unconstrained first-layer interpretation.

changes.before: The construction mirrors the split-pair --- two non-negative streams whose difference is the model --- but with a crucial change of direction: nothing is split; both streams are free to learn any convex (respectively monotone) function, and the difference structure is a training-time inductive bias rather than a post hoc reparameterization. Closely related architectures appeared as convex difference neural networks (CDiNN) in optimal control~\parencite{Sankaranarayanan2021CDINN}, with recurrent extensions for safety-critical model predictive control~\parencite{Chen2025_RCDiNN}; the interpretability perspective developed here is complementary to that line of work. The inverted-input variant is motivated by monotonicity itself: a monotone $h$-stream can only accumulate evidence from the \emph{presence} of input mass, so handing it $\1 - x$ lets it accumulate evidence from what is \emph{missing} in the input.
changes.after: As in the split-pair, two non-negative streams define the model by their difference. Here they learn convex (respectively monotone) functions directly: the difference structure is a training-time inductive bias. Related convex difference neural networks (CDiNN) address optimal control~\parencite{Sankaranarayanan2021CDINN}, with recurrent extensions for safety-critical model predictive control~\parencite{Chen2025_RCDiNN}; we study their interpretability. A monotone $h$-stream accumulates evidence from input mass, so feeding it $\1-x$ lets it respond to missing mass.
changes.reason: Remove repeated training-vs-post-hoc contrast; retain literature scope and complement motivation.

This comparison suggests a useful role for the difference structure, without establishing a general disentanglement property.

changes.before: The two routes of this chapter probe the same structural hypothesis --- that difference-of-monotone representations can make network sensitivities more legible --- from opposite ends. The MNIST study establishes that differences of constrained networks can be trained directly to competitive accuracy. Its visual examples also exhibit class-dependent stream sensitivities on present and candidate missing strokes. These qualitative observations do not establish faithful counterfactual explanations or a general separation of explanatory roles, either for the trained models or for the split-pairs of the pretrained VGG-16 and ResNet-18 models. Evaluating the proposed interpretation through interventions and testing it on larger architectures remain open directions, taken up again in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
changes.after: Both routes test whether difference-of-monotone representations make sensitivities more legible. The MNIST study shows that directly trained differences of constrained networks achieve competitive accuracy and exhibit class-dependent stream sensitivities on present and candidate missing strokes. These qualitative examples establish neither faithful counterfactuals nor general explanatory-role separation for the trained models or pretrained VGG-16/ResNet-18 split-pairs. Complete-model interventions and larger-architecture tests remain open (Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}).
changes.reason: Merge hypothesis/results/limitations; retain both model families and required future tests.

changes.before: The split-based methods above read a fixed \ac{dc} decomposition. The complementary route of Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} attributes through the equilibrium trajectory distribution of the \ac{sg} and \ac{rg}: the per-neuron difference of the two players' discounted occupation measures is the attribution map, and at the anchor temperature $\tau = 1$ this difference recovers the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} family exactly (Theorem~\ref{thm:lrp_recovery}), just as the plain gradient arises as a difference of occupation measures. Those equivalences --- the stopping and routing games, the recovery of gradients and of the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} rule --- are stated in Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory}, with proofs in the companion supplement, and are not restated here. This section collects only what turns those equilibria into concrete, tunable attribution maps: the \emph{modes} that deform the games, and the input-side \emph{technicalities} that raise attribution quality.
changes.after: Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} offers a complementary route to the fixed \ac{dc} readouts: the per-neuron difference of the players' discounted occupation measures under equilibrium trajectories defines attribution. It recovers gradients in the \ac{sg} and the full $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} family in the \ac{rg} at $\tau=1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lrp_recovery}). With these equivalences stated there and proved in the companion supplement, we turn to \emph{modes} that deform the games and input-side \emph{technicalities} that improve their maps.
changes.reason: Replace repeated non-restatement notices and roadmap with recovery theorem and operational scope.

changes.before: Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} deforms the equilibrium trajectory distribution through a small set of orthogonal knobs --- the routing and stopping temperatures $\tau, \theta$, the policy-entropy bonus, the risk parameter $\lambda \le 0$, the stream balance $(\alpha, \beta)$, and the \ac{lrp} stabilizer $\epsilon \ge 0$ --- and establishes an \emph{exact dictionary} (Section~\ref{sec:risk_aversion_regularization}) relating each knob to the backward rule it deforms. We do not restate that dictionary here. What matters for attribution is only the operational role of the knobs: each is a control that turns the abstract game equilibrium into a concrete, tunable attribution map, and together they are the parameters swept in the evaluation of Chapter~\ref{ch:experiments}.
changes.after: Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} varies equilibrium trajectory laws through routing and stopping temperatures $\tau,\theta$, the policy-entropy bonus, risk $\lambda\le0$, stream balance $(\alpha,\beta)$, and \ac{lrp} stabilization $\epsilon\ge0$. Section~\ref{sec:risk_aversion_regularization} gives an exact dictionary from each parameter to its backward rule. These controls yield tunable attribution maps and form the sweeps of Chapter~\ref{ch:experiments}.
changes.reason: Retain all parameters and dictionary/evaluation references while removing duplicated explanation of controls.

changes.before: Two notational cautions specific to this chapter are worth flagging, since two symbols carry a different meaning here than in the split-based methods above. First, the stream balance $(\alpha, \beta)$ --- the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} discount pair, with $\alpha - \beta = 1$ and the theorem-driven anchor $(\alpha, \beta) = (2, 1)$ that reweights support against opposition --- is unrelated to the backward-shift parameter $\alpha \in [0, \tfrac{1}{2}]$ of Section~\ref{sec:split_attribution_concept}; wherever a bare ``$\alpha$'' appears in this section it denotes the \ac{lrp} stream weight. Second, the routing temperature $\tau$ (which recovers $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} exactly only at the anchor $\tau = 1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:lrp_recovery}, and is applied myopically so the recovered forward pass is unchanged) is distinct from the spatial input transforms $\tau_t$ introduced in the Technicalities below.
changes.after: Here $(\alpha,\beta)$ denotes the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} discount pair, with $\alpha-\beta=1$ and anchor $(2,1)$ weighting support against opposition; a bare $\alpha$ is this stream weight, unrelated to the backward shift $\alpha\in[0,\tfrac12]$ of Section~\ref{sec:split_attribution_concept}. Routing temperature $\tau$ recovers $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} exactly only at $\tau=1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lrp_recovery}); its myopic application preserves the forward pass. It is distinct from the spatial transforms $\tau_t$ below.
changes.reason: Condense notation warning; retain distinct alpha meanings, anchor, myopic-forward semantics and transform distinction.

changes.before: A second, orthogonal lever improves the maps on the input side without touching the game: averaging attributions over input transformations, and the detached-operator (DAVE-style) reading of the resulting gradient decomposition. Both matter most on the \ac{vit}, where the $16 \times 16$ patch tokenization breaks translation equivariance and introduces grid artifacts \parencite{Wrobel2024,Dosovitskiy2021vit}.
changes.after: Input-transform averaging and a detached-operator (DAVE-style) reading of the gradient decomposition improve maps without changing the game. They matter especially for \acp{vit}, whose $16\times16$ patch tokenization breaks translation equivariance and introduces grid artifacts~\parencite{Wrobel2024,Dosovitskiy2021vit}.
changes.reason: Simplify input-side mechanism and preserve architecture explanation/citations.

changes.before: \paragraph{Reynolds-inspired averaging.} Following DAVE's transform-averaging strategy \parencite{Wrobel2024}, an attribution is computed on $N$ inputs transformed by random spatial maps $\tau_1, \dots, \tau_N$ --- small rotations, translations, and horizontal flips (distinct from the routing temperature $\tau$ of the games) --- each explanation is mapped back to the original image coordinates by the inverse transform $\tau_t^{-1}$, and the aligned maps are averaged. This Reynolds-inspired averaging can suppress architecture-specific, transform-dependent artifacts while retaining the image-dependent structure common to all transforms; the sample count $N$ trades compute for smoothness and is ablated in Chapter~\ref{ch:experiments}.
changes.after: \paragraph{Reynolds-inspired averaging.} Following DAVE~\parencite{Wrobel2024}, compute attributions on $N$ randomly transformed inputs (small rotations, translations, horizontal flips), map them back by $\tau_t^{-1}$, and average. These spatial transforms $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_N$ are distinct from routing temperature $\tau$. Reynolds-inspired averaging can suppress transform-dependent architectural artifacts while retaining common image structure; $N$ trades computation for smoothness and is ablated in Chapter~\ref{ch:experiments}.
changes.reason: Condense averaging algorithm, retaining transform types, inverse alignment, limited artifact claim and compute tradeoff.
